title: Binning and Binarization
abstract:
Two preprocessing techniques used to transform a continuous numerical feature
into categorical intervals. Binning (discretization) converts a continuous
feature into bins and handles outliers on the way; binarization converts it into
$0/1$ using a threshold. This document covers all the binning strategies from
the notes — unsupervised (equal width, equal frequency, K-Means), supervised
(decision-tree binning) and custom — with the formulas, the
KBinsDiscretizer parameters, why binning buys non-linearity for a linear
model, and the real cost: information loss.

blocks.t: Definitions
From the notes

These are data preprocessing techniques used to transform a continuous
numerical feature into categorical intervals. They help the model
capture meaningful patterns.

items:
Binning (Discretization) — converts a continuous numerical
 feature into categorical bins. Handles outliers.

Binarization — converts a numerical feature into
 binary $(0/1)$ using a threshold.

blocks.t: Why bins at all

The notes' justification: few real-world behaviours happen in ranges.
Example: salary ranges (Low, Med, High) instead of exact values. Nobody
behaves differently at a salary of ₹$74{,}000$ versus
₹$74{,}100$; they behave differently in a bracket. Tax systems,
insurance premiums, and age-based marketing all work in brackets, so encoding
the bracket directly matches the real generating process.
Types of Binning

Supervised

blocks.cap:
The same bimodal age column cut into six bins by each unsupervised
 strategy. Equal width gives bins of identical span but wildly unequal counts;
 equal frequency gives identical counts but unequal spans; K-Means places
 boundaries where the data is sparse.

blocks.t: Equal Width / Uniform Binning
From the notes
You choose the bin count, e.g. $\text{bins}=10$.
\boxed{ \text{bin width}=\frac{\max-\min}{\text{bins}} }

Example: $\max=100$, $\min=0$, $\text{bins}=10$ $\Rightarrow$ 10 bins of interval
10 each.
The notes' key observation

No change in the spread of the data, but it handles outliers. The
distribution's shape is preserved — if 80% of your data sits between 20 and 30,
80% still lands in one bin. But an extreme value at 500 simply falls into the
top bin instead of dominating a distance or a coefficient.

Weakness: on skewed data, most bins are empty and one bin holds nearly
everything, so the encoding carries almost no information.
Equal Frequency / Quantile Binning
From the notes

Suppose $\text{bins}=10$. Each interval will contain 10% of the total
observations — this is percentile-based.
Worked from the notes: intervals $0$–$16$, $16$–$20$, $20$–$22$.
From the notes

The binning size is not equal. This is used more. Each bin holds the
same number of rows, not the same range — which is why the bin
widths shrink where the data is dense and stretch where it is sparse.

This is the workhorse. It guarantees every bin has enough observations to
estimate a stable effect, and it is naturally robust to skew and outliers,
because the boundaries are quantiles.
K-Means Binning
From the notes

Used when data is spread in clusters. Clustering is done and each bin
acts as a cluster.

1-D K-Means finds $k$ centroids and the bin edges are the midpoints between
adjacent centroids. On genuinely multimodal data — two age groups, two price
tiers — this places boundaries in the sparse valleys between the modes, which
neither equal-width nor equal-frequency will do.
Decision Tree Binning (supervised)

The only supervised strategy: it uses the target. Fit a shallow decision
tree on the single feature against $y$ and take the tree's split thresholds as
bin edges. Because the tree chooses splits to maximise information gain
(Topic 55), the resulting bins are optimal with respect to the target
rather than to the feature's own distribution.
Supervised binning can leak

It uses $y$, so it must be fitted inside cross-validation folds like any other
learned transformer. Fitting the tree on the full dataset and then
cross-validating produces optimistic scores for exactly the reason described in
Topic 17.
Custom Binning
From the notes

Use your own knowledge or domain knowledge for binning.
Cannot be done using scikit-learn — use pandas custom code.

pd.cut with explicit edges. This is often the best option: age brackets
$0$–$12$, $13$–$19$, $20$–$35$, $36$–$60$, $60+$ encode real developmental and
economic stages that no unsupervised algorithm will discover.
How Binning Works in Scikit-learn
From the notes: KBinsDiscretizer()
Parameters used:
Choosing encode

ordinal gives one column of integers $0,1,2,\ldots$ — correct, because
bins are ordered. onehot gives one binary column per bin, which
frees a linear model to give each bin an independent coefficient rather than
assuming the effect is monotone across bins. Use onehot when you binned
specifically to capture a non-monotone shape.
Why Binning Helps — and What It Costs

blocks.cap:
Accident risk is U-shaped in age — high for the young, low in
 middle age, high again for the elderly. A linear model fits a flat, useless
 line. After binning, each bracket gets its own effect and the shape is
 recovered.

head: Benefits
Costs
rows: Captures non-linear and non-monotone relationships in a linear model
Handles outliers (they fall into the end bin)
Arbitrary boundaries: 29.9 and 30.1 land in different bins
Reduces the effect of noise and small measurement errors
Reduces statistical power; you spend degrees of freedom
Makes the feature interpretable to a business audience
Bin count is a hyperparameter you must tune
Handles missing values naturally as their own bin
Tree models gain nothing — they already bin internally

blocks.t: Do not bin for a tree-based model

A decision tree already discretises every continuous feature by choosing split
thresholds, and it chooses them optimally with respect to the target. Pre-binning
takes that freedom away and can only hurt. Binning is a technique for
linear models — and for interpretability.
Binarization
From the notes

Converts a numerical feature into binary $(0/1)$ using a threshold.
Example: Income $>50{,}000 \to 1$ else $0$.

blocks.cap:
Left: binarization is a single cut. Right: quantile binning absorbs
 extreme incomes into the top bin — an income of 12M and one of 200k both land
 in bin 4, which is exactly the outlier-handling property the notes highlight.

blocks.t:
Binarization is binning with $\text{bins}=2$ and a threshold you choose. It is
the right tool when the domain genuinely has a cliff — a regulatory limit, a
free-shipping threshold, a pass mark — and the wrong tool when you are merely
guessing at where the effect changes.
Code

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import KBinsDiscretizer, Binarizer, FunctionTransformer
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline, make_pipeline
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, LogisticRegression
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor, DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, train_test_split

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
age = np.clip(np.r_[rng.normal(28, 6, 600), rng.normal(52, 9, 400)], 18, 90)
X = age.reshape(-1, 1)

# =====================================================================
# 1. EQUAL WIDTH -- the notes' formula, verified
# =====================================================================
bins = 10
width = (age.max() - age.min()) / bins
print(f"max {age.max():.1f}  min {age.min():.1f}  bins {bins}  width {width:.2f}")

uni = KBinsDiscretizer(n_bins=bins, encode="ordinal", strategy="uniform").fit(X)
edges = uni.bin_edges_[0]
print("edges:", edges.round(1))
print("all widths equal:", np.allclose(np.diff(edges), width))
print("counts per bin:", np.histogram(age, edges)[0])
# Equal SPANS, very unequal COUNTS -- the weakness of uniform binning.

# =====================================================================
# 2. EQUAL FREQUENCY -- each bin holds 10% of the observations
# =====================================================================
qua = KBinsDiscretizer(n_bins=10, encode="ordinal", strategy="quantile").fit(X)
print("counts per bin:", np.histogram(age, qua.bin_edges_[0])[0])   # all ~100
print("widths:", np.diff(qua.bin_edges_[0]).round(2))               # very unequal
# Equal COUNTS, unequal SPANS. "This is used more." -- the notes.

# The pandas equivalent, which returns readable interval labels:
print(pd.qcut(age, q=10).value_counts().sort_index().head(3))

# =====================================================================
# 3. K-MEANS BINNING -- boundaries land in the sparse valleys
# =====================================================================
km = KBinsDiscretizer(n_bins=4, encode="ordinal", strategy="kmeans").fit(X)
print("kmeans edges:", km.bin_edges_[0].round(1))
# On this bimodal data one edge sits between the two modes (~40),
# which neither uniform nor quantile binning would place there.

# =====================================================================
# 4. CUSTOM BINNING -- pandas, because sklearn cannot express domain rules
# =====================================================================
labels = ["child", "teen", "young_adult", "adult", "senior"]
custom = pd.cut(age, bins=[0, 12, 19, 35, 60, 120], labels=labels)
print(custom.value_counts().sort_index())

# Wrap it so it still lives inside a pipeline:
def bin_age(a):
    return pd.cut(np.asarray(a).ravel(), bins=[0, 12, 19, 35, 60, 120],
                  labels=False).reshape(-1, 1)
custom_tf = FunctionTransformer(bin_age)
print("as a transformer:", custom_tf.fit_transform(X)[:5].ravel())

# =====================================================================
# 5. SUPERVISED: DECISION TREE BINNING -- the target picks the edges
# =====================================================================
y_risk = np.where(age < 25, 0.55, np.where(age < 60, 0.15, 0.65)) \
         + rng.normal(0, .05, len(age))

tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_leaf_nodes=4, random_state=0).fit(X, y_risk)
thr = np.sort(tree.tree_.threshold[tree.tree_.feature >= 0])
print("tree-chosen edges:", thr.round(1))       # lands near 25 and 60 -- correct
# Compare: quantile binning would place edges at the population percentiles,
# which have nothing to do with where the RISK actually changes.

class TreeBinner:
    """Supervised binning. MUST be fitted inside CV folds -- it uses y."""
    def __init__(self, max_leaf_nodes=5):
        self.max_leaf_nodes = max_leaf_nodes
    def fit(self, X, y):
        t = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_leaf_nodes=self.max_leaf_nodes,
                                  random_state=0).fit(X, y)
        thr = t.tree_.threshold[t.tree_.feature >= 0]
        self.edges_ = np.r_[-np.inf, np.sort(thr), np.inf]
        return self
    def transform(self, X):
        return np.digitize(np.asarray(X).ravel(), self.edges_[1:-1]).reshape(-1, 1)
    def fit_transform(self, X, y=None):
        return self.fit(X, y).transform(X)

# =====================================================================
# 6. DOES BINNING ACTUALLY HELP? -- the U-shape experiment
# =====================================================================
plain = LinearRegression()
binned = make_pipeline(
    KBinsDiscretizer(n_bins=8, encode="onehot-dense", strategy="quantile"),
    LinearRegression())

print("linear on raw age   R2:", cross_val_score(plain,  X, y_risk, cv=5).mean().round(3))
print("linear on binned age R2:", cross_val_score(binned, X, y_risk, cv=5).mean().round(3))
# ~0.00 vs ~0.85 -- the linear model literally cannot see a U-shape otherwise.

# encode="ordinal" would NOT fix it: it forces a monotone effect across bins.
ordinal_pipe = make_pipeline(
    KBinsDiscretizer(n_bins=8, encode="ordinal", strategy="quantile"),
    LinearRegression())
print("ordinal encoding    R2:", cross_val_score(ordinal_pipe, X, y_risk, cv=5).mean().round(3))
# Use encode="onehot" when the relationship is NON-MONOTONE.

# =====================================================================
# 7. AND WHERE IT DOES NOT HELP -- trees
# =====================================================================
tree_raw = DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=4, random_state=0)
tree_bin = make_pipeline(KBinsDiscretizer(n_bins=8, encode="ordinal",
                                          strategy="quantile"),
                         DecisionTreeRegressor(max_depth=4, random_state=0))
print("tree raw    R2:", cross_val_score(tree_raw, X, y_risk, cv=5).mean().round(3))
print("tree binned R2:", cross_val_score(tree_bin, X, y_risk, cv=5).mean().round(3))
# Essentially identical, often slightly WORSE binned -- you removed the tree's
# freedom to choose its own thresholds.

# =====================================================================
# 8. BINARIZATION
# =====================================================================
income = np.r_[rng.lognormal(10.6, .5, 900), [5e6, 8e6, 1.2e7]]
b = Binarizer(threshold=50_000).fit_transform(income.reshape(-1, 1))
print("above 50k:", int(b.sum()), "of", len(income))

# equivalently, and more readably for a single rule:
print("same result:", np.array_equal(b.ravel(), (income > 50_000).astype(float)))

# Binning ABSORBS the outliers -- the notes' "handles outliers" claim:
kb = KBinsDiscretizer(n_bins=5, encode="ordinal", strategy="quantile")
codes = kb.fit_transform(income.reshape(-1, 1)).ravel()
print("bin of a 12M income:", codes[-1], " bin of a 200k income:",
      codes[np.argmin(np.abs(income - 200_000))])
# Both land in the top bin. A raw 12M value would have dominated any
# distance or coefficient; the binned value cannot.

# =====================================================================
# 9. IN A REAL PIPELINE, AND TUNING THE BIN COUNT
# =====================================================================
df = pd.DataFrame({"age": age, "income": rng.lognormal(10.5, .6, len(age))})
yb = (y_risk > y_risk.mean()).astype(int)

pre = ColumnTransformer([
    ("age_bins", KBinsDiscretizer(n_bins=8, encode="onehot-dense",
                                  strategy="quantile"), ["age"]),
    ("inc_bins", KBinsDiscretizer(n_bins=5, encode="ordinal",
                                  strategy="quantile"), ["income"]),
])
pipe = Pipeline([("pre", pre), ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))])

from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV
gs = GridSearchCV(pipe, {
    "pre__age_bins__n_bins":   [4, 6, 8, 12, 20],
    "pre__age_bins__strategy": ["uniform", "quantile", "kmeans"],
}, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=-1).fit(df, yb)
print("best binning:", gs.best_params_, round(gs.best_score_, 4))
# n_bins is a hyperparameter. Too few -> information loss.
# Too many -> back to a continuous feature, with noise.
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
Both techniques transform a continuous numerical feature into
 categorical intervals, to help the model capture meaningful patterns.

Binning (discretization) converts continuous $\to$ categorical
 bins and handles outliers. Binarization converts
 numerical $\to$ binary $(0/1)$ using a threshold.

Unsupervised: Equal Width (uniform), Equal Frequency
 (quantile), K-Means. Supervised: Decision Tree binning.
 Custom: your own domain rules.

Equal width: $\text{width}=\frac{\max-\min}{\text{bins}}$.
 No change in the spread of data, but it handles outliers.

Equal frequency: each bin contains $\frac{100}{\text{bins}}\%$
 of observations. Bin sizes are unequal. This is used more.

K-Means: used when data is spread in clusters; each bin acts as
 a cluster.

Custom binning cannot be done in scikit-learn — use pandas
 (pd.cut).

KBinsDiscretizer(n_bins, strategy={uniform, quantile, kmeans},
 encode={ordinal, onehot}). Use onehot for non-monotone effects.

Binning buys non-linearity for a linear model. It gains nothing for
 trees, which already discretise optimally.
The cost is information loss and arbitrary boundaries.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Equal width or equal frequency — which and why?

Equal frequency in most cases: every bin gets enough observations to estimate a
stable effect, and it is naturally robust to skew and outliers because the
boundaries are quantiles. Equal width when the bins must be interpretable in
domain units — age decades, price bands a customer would recognise.

Q. Why would you bin a feature at all? Isn't it throwing information
away?

Yes, and that is sometimes the point. You gain the ability to capture a
non-linear or non-monotone relationship in a linear model, robustness to
outliers, and interpretability. You lose granularity and statistical power. Bin
when the real-world effect genuinely operates in brackets.
Q. Should you bin features before XGBoost?

No. Trees choose their own split thresholds, and they choose them optimally with
respect to the target. Pre-binning removes that freedom and can only hurt.

Q. You binned age and results got worse with encode="ordinal".
Why?

Ordinal encoding gives the bins integer codes, so a linear model fits a single
slope across them — it still assumes a monotone effect. If you binned to capture
a U-shape, use encode="onehot" so each bin gets its own coefficient.
Q. How do you choose the number of bins?

Treat it as a hyperparameter and tune it by cross-validation. Too few loses real
signal; too many recreates the continuous feature and refits noise. Also require
a minimum count per bin — typically a few dozen rows — so each bin's effect is
estimable.
Q. What is the risk of supervised (decision-tree) binning?

It uses the target, so it leaks if fitted outside the cross-validation loop. It
must sit inside a pipeline and be refitted on each fold's training data.
